Bloomberg published an article highlighting the staggering returns Apple shareholders have received during Tim Cook's tenure as CEO. The cumulative gain reached 2,275%, and with dividends factored in, the total return climbed to 2,736%.

The article suggests this will make it difficult for any successor to match. But in my view, incoming CEO John Ternus does not need to deliberately emulate Cook's management style...

The numbers Bloomberg cites are indisputable.

My position is simply that Ternus shouldn't lose any sleep over whether Apple can replicate those same financial results under his leadership — for two reasons.

First, both of his main predecessors believed financial success was a byproduct of the real goal, not something to chase directly. Steve Jobs famously said:

Cook himself has echoed that philosophy, saying he never worried about quarterly results and instead focused on the company's long-term direction.

Second, there's the advice Steve gave when he handed the baton to Tim:

Ternus shouldn't ask himself what Jobs or Cook would do, but instead should run Apple in the way he believes is most likely to produce the best products, and shape the corporate culture and values most conducive to long-term success.

I expect him to be a very different CEO from Cook, just as Cook was different from Jobs. The point isn't to try to replicate the formula for past success, but to look to the future — to borrow a phrase from that outgoing CEO — and follow your own North Star.

Do you agree with my take, or do you see it differently? Let us know in the comments.
